extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and researchers learning algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, criteria, and standard results about Hilbert functions/polynomials, degree and genus, Serre's cohomological criteria (ampleness, affineness), and properties of higher direct images/pushforwards for projective morphisms. Includes exercises giving standard reduction tricks and example computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function eventual polynomiality (Theorem 18.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a coherent sheaf on a projective k-scheme X ⊂ P^n_k, then χ(X, F(m)) is a polynomial in m whose degree equals dim Supp F; consequently for m ≫ 0, h^0(X, F(m)) agrees with a polynomial p_F(m) of that degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Serre vanishing to kill higher cohomology for large twists. The result is used repeatedly; reduce to algebraically closed/ infinite base field as needed. Exercises show how to reduce degree by slicing with a hyperplane that avoids associated points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Hilbert polynomial (18.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The polynomial p_F(m) := χ(X, F(m)) for m ≫ 0 is called the Hilbert polynomial of the coherent sheaf F. For a projective scheme X, p_X(m) := p_{O_X}(m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of p_F equals dim Supp F; degree −1 is used to encode the zero sheaf. Examples (Pn, hypersurfaces, Veronese, twisted cubic) illustrate computation methods using exact sequences and projection formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a projective scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective k-scheme X of dimension n, the degree is defined to be n! times the leading coefficient of the Hilbert polynomial p_X(m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: degree(P^n)=1, twisted cubic degree=3. Exercises show degree is integer (18.6.G) and compute degrees of hypersurfaces and Veronese embeddings. Bézout-type results relate intersection degrees to products of degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic genus (from Hilbert polynomial)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arithmetic genus of X is 1 − p_X(0) = 1 − χ(X, O_X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For projective curves in P^2 of degree d, plugging m=0 in p_C gives h^1(C,O_C) and hence arithmetic genus; used to distinguish many curves from P^1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's cohomological criterion for ampleness (Theorem 18.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian ring A, proper A-scheme X, and invertible sheaf L on X, the following are equivalent: (a–c) L is ample on X (the standard projective/global-generation/Zariski-topology characterizations), and (e) for every coherent sheaf F on X there is n_0 such that H^i(X, F ⊗ L^{⊗ n}) = 0 for all i > 0 and all n ≥ n_0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a cohomological test for ampleness: vanishing of higher cohomology of all coherent sheaves after high enough positive twists. The proof shows (a–c)⇒(e) by choosing a very ample power and applying Serre vanishing; (e)⇒ampleness is proven by showing L^{⊗ n} is globally generated for n ≫ 0 using local vanishing at closed points and patching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's cohomological characterization of affineness (Theorem 18.7.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian separated scheme X the following are equivalent: (a) X is affine; (b) for any quasicoherent sheaf F on X, H^i(X, F)=0 for all i>0; (c) for any coherent sheaf of ideals I on X, H^1(X, I)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanishing of higher cohomology of (quasi)coherent sheaves characterizes affineness. The nontrivial implication is (c)⇒(a). Analogue: Stein spaces in complex analytic geometry are characterized similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of higher pushforward sheaves (Theorem 18.8.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quasicompact separated morphism π: X → Y and a quasicoherent F on X: (a) R^i π_* F are quasicoherent sheaves on Y; (b) R^0 π_* = π_*; (c) a short exact sequence 0→F→G→H→0 induces the usual long exact sequence of R^i π_*; (d) if π is projective and O_Y coherent and F coherent then each R^i π_* F is coherent (Grothendieck's coherence theorem for projective morphisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses Cech cohomology and localization; all assertions can be checked on affine opens. The coherence statement requires projectivity (and Y locally Noetherian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative dimensional cohomology vanishing (Theorem 18.8.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is projective and Y is locally Noetherian (or O_Y coherent), then R^i π_* F = 0 for i greater than the maximum dimension of the fibers of π (for any quasicoherent F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes dimension bounds for cohomology of projective schemes to relative settings; the projective hypothesis is essential (counterexamples exist for nonprojective morphisms). The proof reduces to a neighborhood of a point and uses an affine cover of the fiber to bound cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine morphism higher pushforward vanishing (18.8.A Easy Exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π is affine, then R^i π_* F = 0 for all i > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from definition: cohomology on affine schemes vanishes in positive degrees for quasicoherent sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base change for higher pushforwards (Exercise 18.8.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For a Cartesian square with ψ: Z→Y and π: X→Y, there is a natural morphism ψ^*(R^i π_* F) → R^i π'_* (ψ'^* F). (b) If ψ is affine and flat (e.g., affine flat base change), then this natural morphism is an isomorphism (cohomology commutes with affine flat base change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FHHF theorem (cohomology commutes with localization) is the technical input. Special cases include formation of fibers and maps from stalks: there is always a natural map (R^i π_* F) ⊗ κ(q) → H^i(π^{-1}(q), F|_{π^{-1}(q)}), which is an isomorphism under good hypotheses (Cohomology and Base Change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection formula for higher pushforwards (Exercise 18.8.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X→Y quasicompact separated, and quasicoherent F on X and G on Y, there is a natural morphism (R^i π_* F) ⊗ G → R^i π_* (F ⊗ π^* G). If G is locally free then this morphism is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct using FHHF; the isomorphism when G is locally free is a standard projection formula generalization to higher direct images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperplane section trick avoiding associated points (Exercise 18.6.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective over an infinite field k and F a coherent sheaf, then for a very ample line bundle L=O(1) there exists an effective Cartier divisor D (a hyperplane) not meeting the associated points of F; multiplication by its section x gives an injective map F(-1) → F and hence a short exact sequence 0→F(-1)→F→G→0 with Supp G = Supp F ∩ V(x), so dim Supp G = dim Supp F - 1 (unless F=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard inductive tool to reduce the dimension of support in proofs about Hilbert polynomials; relies on the infinitude of k to choose a hyperplane missing finitely many points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial difference lemma (Exercise 18.6.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If functions f and g on integers satisfy f(m+1) − f(m) = g(m), and g is a polynomial of degree d ≥ 0, then f is a polynomial of degree d+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the inductive argument showing χ(X,F(m)) is a polynomial: the difference of Hilbert polynomials reduces degree by 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bézout's theorem for degree (Exercise 18.6.K)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a projective scheme of dimension ≥1 and H is a hypersurface not containing any associated points of X, then deg(H ∩ X) = (deg H) (deg X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specializes to plane curves: two plane curves of degrees m and n with no common components meet in mn points counted with multiplicity. Requires that H avoid embedded/associated components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity of degree for unions (Exercise 18.6.P)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are d-dimensional closed subschemes of P^n_k with no d-dimensional irreducible components in common, then deg(X ∪ Y) = deg X + deg Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree behaves additively on unions without overlapping top-dimensional components; useful in decomposition arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and computations of Hilbert polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples given: p_{P^n}(m) = binomial(m+n, n) (interpreted as polynomial), for a degree d hypersurface H ⊂ P^n we have p_H(m)=p_{P^n}(m) − p_{P^n}(m−d); the twisted cubic (image of P^1 by |O(3)| in P^3) has Hilbert polynomial 3m+1; the d-th Veronese embedding Hilbert polynomial and degree computations follow similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute via short exact sequences coming from embeddings (ideal sheaf sequences) and use projection formula or direct transition function arguments. Exercises guide explicit checks (twisted cubic, Veronese).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete intersections: genus and connectivity (Exercises 18.6.Q–T)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises ask for (Q) genus of intersection of two quadric surfaces in P^3, (R) genus of complete intersection of surfaces of degrees m and n in P^3 (e.g., m=2,n=3 gives genus 4), (S) rational normal curve of degree d is not a complete intersection if d>2, (T) positive-dimensional complete intersections are connected (show h^0(O_X)=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Hilbert polynomial computations, Bézout, and cohomological arguments (e.g., h^0 preservation under field extension) and Riemann-Roch for curves. Bertini's theorem guarantees regular examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples and cautions about hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Several statements emphasize necessary hypotheses: e.g., projectivity (not merely quasi-projectivity) is essential for relative dimensional vanishing; properness in ampleness criterion; infinitude of base field in the hyperplane-avoidance argument. Explicit exercises exhibit failures when hypotheses are dropped (e.g., open embedding A^n−{0} into A^n breaks relative vanishing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always verify the required hypotheses (Noetherian, projective, proper, base-field infinite/ algebraically closed, flatness for base-change theorems) before applying the theorems; exercises give concrete failure modes.
